title: Central tendency recap: mean, median and mode
summary: A quick recap from this deck's slides: how to find the mean, median and mode, with the Players' Problem and the odd and even median examples.

chunks.heading: Mean (sample and population)
chunks.explanation_md:
**Measures of central tendency:** the **mean**, **median** and **mode** (the agenda also lists percentiles and quartiles).

The **(arithmetic) mean**, also known as the average, is the **sum of the values divided by the number of values**. The **sample mean x̄** is the point estimator of the **population mean μ**.

- **Sample mean:** x̄ = Σxi / n (n = number of observations in the sample)
- **Population mean:** μ = Σxi / N (N = number of observations in the population)

Class activity: calculate the population mean and the sample mean of the class heights.

key_terms.meaning: The sum of the values divided by the number of values; also called the average.
A sample statistic used to estimate a population value; the sample mean x̄ estimates the population mean μ.

chunks.exam_line: Sample mean x̄ = Σxi/n; population mean μ = Σxi/N. x̄ is the point estimator of μ.

chunks.heading: Median (odd and even number of values)
chunks.explanation_md:
The **median** is the **middle value when the data are arranged in ascending order**.

- **Odd number of observations:** the median is the middle value. The 7 values 26, 18, 27, 12, 14, 27, 19 sort to 12, 14, 18, 19, 26, 27, 27, so **Median = 19**.
- **Even number of observations:** the median is the **average of the middle two values**. The 8 values 26, 18, 27, 12, 14, 27, 30, 19 sort to 12, 14, 18, 19, 26, 27, 27, 30, so **Median = (19 + 26)/2 = 22.5**.

**Why use it:** when a data set has **extreme values**, the median is the preferred measure of central location. It is the measure most often (not always) reported for **annual income and property value data**, because a few extremely large incomes or values can **inflate the mean**.

key_terms.meaning: The value in the middle when the data items are arranged in ascending order.

chunks.exam_line: Median: sort, then middle value (odd n) or average of the middle two (even n). Preferred when there are extreme values. Examples: 19; (19 + 26)/2 = 22.5.

A few extremely large incomes can inflate the mean but not the median.

chunks.heading: Mode, and the Players' Problem
chunks.explanation_md:
The **mode** is the **value that occurs with the greatest frequency**. The greatest frequency can occur at two or more values: exactly two modes means **bimodal**; more than two means **multimodal**.

**Players' Problem (runs in 20 matches each, total 655 for both):** the mean for both is 32.75, but Player-1 has median 10 and mode 4 while Player-2 has median 30.5 and mode 45. The averages tell different stories, which is why the professor asks what you observe from mean, median and mode.

**Frequency table and dot plot:** the value 18 occurs 4 times (the mode), the median is near 22 and the mean is 26.9. Because a few high values (49, 52, 56) sit far to the right, the mean (26.9) is pulled above the median.

key_terms.meaning: The value that occurs with the greatest frequency.
A data set with exactly two modes.
A data set with more than two modes.

chunks.exam_line: Mode = most frequent value; two modes = bimodal; more than two = multimodal. Players: same mean 32.75, medians 10 and 30.5, modes 4 and 45.

questions.stem: Write the formulas for the sample mean and population mean and explain the symbols.
questions.model_answer_md:
- **Sample mean:** x̄ = Σxi / n, where n is the number of observations in the sample.
- **Population mean:** μ = Σxi / N, where N is the number of observations in the population.

The sample mean x̄ is the point estimator of the population mean μ.

questions.stem: Find the median of 26, 18, 27, 12, 14, 27, 30, 19 and of the first seven of these values without 30.
questions.model_answer_md:
Sort the eight values: 12, 14, 18, 19, 26, 27, 27, 30. Even count, so average the middle two: (19 + 26)/2 = **22.5**.

Without 30 the seven values sort to 12, 14, 18, 19, 26, 27, 27; the median is the middle value, **19**.

questions.stem: Both players in the Players' Problem have mean 32.75, but Player-1 has median 10 and mode 4 while Player-2 has median 30.5 and mode 45. What do you observe?
questions.model_answer_md:
The **means are equal**, so the average hides a difference. Player-1's **median (10) is far below the mean (32.75)**: a few very large scores lift the mean, so most matches are low scores and the mode 4 agrees. Player-2's median (30.5) is close to the mean, so the scores are balanced, though the mode of 45 shows a peak at high scores.

So the three measures together show Player-1 is skewed and Player-2 is steady.

rubric.point: Player-1 median far below mean: skewed by large scores

questions.stem: Explain the mean, median and mode: definitions, how each is found, and when the median is preferred.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Introduction.** These are the three measures of central tendency.

**Mean.** Also the average: the sum of the values divided by the number of values. Sample x̄ = Σxi/n; population μ = Σxi/N. x̄ is the point estimator of μ.

**Median.** The middle value when data are in ascending order. For an odd count it is the middle value (19 for 12, 14, 18, 19, 26, 27, 27); for an even count it is the average of the middle two ((19 + 26)/2 = 22.5).

**Mode.** The value with the greatest frequency. Two modes make the data bimodal; more than two, multimodal.

**When to prefer the median.** When there are extreme values, because a few extremely large incomes or property values can inflate the mean. It is the measure most often reported for annual income and property value data.

**Conclusion.** Choose the measure to suit the data, and report which one you used.

rubric.point: Median with odd and even examples

questions.stem: Use the Players' Problem to show why mean, median and mode must be read together and why spread is also needed.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Data.** Each player has 20 scores and both total 655, so each mean is 32.75.

**Median and mode.** Player-1: median 10, mode 4. Player-2: median 30.5, mode 45.

**Reading together.** For Player-1 the mean (32.75) is much larger than the median (10), because a few big scores (such as 90 and 78) pull it up; the typical match is a low score. For Player-2 mean and median are close, so the scores are balanced.

**Why spread is needed.** The averages differ in story, but a number for spread makes it clear: the range is 90 for Player-1 and 20 for Player-2. Player-2 is much more consistent.

**Conclusion.** One average can mislead; compare mean, median, mode and then a measure of variability before judging performance.

rubric.point: Mean pulled by large scores for Player-1
